Problem Statement 26 27 ### 1.1 Context 28 29 The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all 30 server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to 31 integrated systems. That layer currently serves three integration touchpoints: SLAS token 32 validation, payment method metadata, and Marketing Cloud email. Two proxy origins are configured, 33 SCAPI and OCAPI. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme 34 (`.docs/integration/`), with the remainder still to be built. Integration build-out begins in the 35 coming sprints. 36 37 ### 1.2 Problem 38 39 How many MRT applications the storefront deploys, and how integration code is divided across them, 40 has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not 41 a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology 42 determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive 43 to change once integration code exists across many systems. 44 45 Compounding this, the safeguards that would contain a failing integration are largely absent. Node's 46 `fetch` does isolate connections per upstream origin by default, so one slow integration does not 47 starve another's connections. What is missing sits above that layer: per-origin connection limits and 48 response timeouts are unset, integration modules do not consistently catch their own failures, and 49 three route handlers start work whose outcome nothing observes. Seven per-origin connection pools 50 were written to address part of this (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported 51 nowhere and attached to no request. All of this is present-state fact, verified in code, and for the 52 in-process failure behaviours by test (§6), not a projection. 53 54 ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved 55 56 - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed 57 position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever 58 writes the first proxy. 59 - The missing error handling persists and compounds. It was found by chance in one of the only three 60 server-side integration touchpoints that exist today, and nothing in the codebase, review process, 61 or CI prevents the same pattern recurring as the remaining systems are built. 62 - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback 63 that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. 64 - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking 65 divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. 66 67 ### 1.4 Success Criteria 68 69 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how 70 integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 71 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, 72 with any inaccuracies in existing documentation identified and raised for correction (§7). 73 3. The present failure behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than 74 asserted. The isolation behaviour of the implemented design cannot be demonstrated until §5 75 ships; that test is specified in §6.1 and is a deliverable of the implementing ticket. 76 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without 77 re-opening the question. 78 79 --- 80 81 ## 2. Options Analysis 107 108 ### 3.1 Options Summary 109 110 | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | 111 | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | 112 | **Option A**: Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost, since it is the current state.

All 120 integration code (proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls) lives inside that single 121 Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by 122 construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one 123 hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its 124 weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than 125 infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). 126 127 #### Option B: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* 128 129 The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as 130 its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and 131 credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses 132 precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised 133 specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. 134 135 It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or 136 budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications 137 created from a PWA Kit template, a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle, and is not a 138 general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as 139 an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent 140 directions. First, the platform documentation's own constraint statement. Second, Salesforce's own 141 B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable 142 Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for 143 backend integration logic (an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an 144 externally-hosted API) with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. Third, firsthand in 145 Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment 146 defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a 147 storefront. 148 149 MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose: separating distinct brands or 150 domains, each of which is itself a full storefront, not decomposing one storefront's backend. 151 Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently 152 count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every 153 cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and 154 the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight 155 storefronts depend on. 156 157 The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and 158 the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. 159 160 --- 161 162 ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale 163 164 ### 4.1 Recommended Option 165 166 **Option A: Single MRT application, with per-integration safeguards in the server-side layer.** 167 168 ### 4.2 Rationale 169 170 Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off 171 between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an 172 integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A 173 is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost 174 because it is the current state. 175 176 The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of 177 the status quo, because the status quo includes gaps that are real and demonstrated: integration 178 modules do not consistently catch their own failures, three route handlers leave work unobserved, and 179 no upstream call carries a timeout short enough to fail before MRT's own execution ceiling does. 180 Option A is therefore recommended **with safeguards**: one bundle, but with each integration confined to its own module, 181 given its own connection pool with an independent connection cap and timeout budget, wrapped in its 182 own error boundary, and with every route registration observing the promise it starts. These are 183 specified in §5. Adopting Option A without them would settle the topology question while leaving the 184 isolation gap open, which is the state this document exists to close. 185 186 ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted 187 188 - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do 189 not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any 190 integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or 191 configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by 192 infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. 193 - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of 194 deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every 195 integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. 196 - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat 197 environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing: anyone 198 who needs deploy or variable access for one integration necessarily has it for all of them. The 199 platform provides no way to scope either within a single project. Accepted; revisit if the team 200 composition changes such that per-integration scoping becomes necessary. 201 - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the 202 module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. 203 204 --- 205 206 ## 5. Technical Implementation 207 208 > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in 220 `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 221 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under 222 `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 223 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its 224 own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is 225 capped independently of every other integration. 226 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a 227 slow upstream can hold a connection, and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution 228 ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 229 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 230 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it 231 at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome: an HTTP error response for a 232 dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful 233 degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 234 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the **entire** promise 235 chain it starts, not merely its final call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved 236 floating promise. Three layers: **Vitest** (unit logic) · **Storybook** `play` (component interactions) · **Playwright** (E2E). Write tests only where failure would be non-obvious or costly to debug — data mapping, integration boundaries, complex state, and pure logic that would survive a refactor invisibly if broken. Every UI component needs a `.stories.tsx`; every logic-heavy feature needs a `.test.ts` or a story `play`.

Full layer guidance, file layout, selector priority, and mocking policy: [.claude/rules/testing.md](.claude/rules/testing.md). (The no-MSW rule in Rules applies to production paths only.)

## Graceful Degradation

Each external system must fail independently — one outage must not break the whole page. Two defaults override any per-system behaviour: **fail closed on consent** (if consent state is unknown, load no third-party scripts), and **never silently substitute a different checkout, payment, or commerce flow** when an integration is down — surface an explicit error instead.

## Performance

Mobile page speed is a top priority. Every change that touches rendering, data fetching, or assets must not regress it.

- **LCP budget is tight (≤ 2s at p75 mobile)** — Defer every third-party script that isn't required for first paint. Anything loaded via Didomi callback (GTM, Optimizely, Inside Chat, Narvar EDD, reCAPTCHA, etc.) must not block LCP — use `defer`, `async`, or post-hydration injection. If a new third-party integration looks like it might land on the critical path, flag it before merging.
- **Images:** Always use lazy loading and serve correctly sized images. Never render full-resolution images at thumbnail size.
- **Code splitting:** Prefer dynamic `import()` for heavy components not needed on initial render.
- **Data fetching:** Avoid over-fetching — request only the fields you need. Waterfall requests are not acceptable; parallelise where possible.
- **Bundle size:** Do not introduce large dependencies without confirming with the user.
- **Dependencies:** Before implementing any feature that may require a third-party library, check `package.json` for what is already installed. Evaluate whether an existing dependency can satisfy the requirement. If a better third-party option exists, present the recommendation (existing vs. new, with trade-offs) and wait for user approval before installing anything.

## Gotchas

- **Theme runtime errors:** Custom components (e.g. `ListMenu`) must be defined in the theme object or destructuring will throw.
- **Commerce SDK types not importable:** Check `node_modules/commerce-sdk-isomorphic/dist/` for generated definitions, or declare a narrow local `type`.
- **Magento password migration:** Passwords were not migrated from Magento — all existing customers must reset at go-live. Do not assume any saved credentials exist. Account creation and login flows must handle this gracefully (CFD-013).

## Requirements

Requirements for this project are in `.docs/`, they must be strictly followed.
Before any code changes, verify logic against relevant `.docs/` files.
For any task that touches an external integration, check the matching `.docs/integration/NN-*.md` doc.

If a requirement is missing, ambiguous, or not yet confirmed — **stop, flag the ambiguity, propose a solution, and wait for user approval before proceeding.** Do not fill gaps with assumptions.

Verification: Start every task by briefly stating which doc/section you are following (e.g. "Implementing per auth.md section 2.1" or "Implementing per 07-adyen.md §3").

**Doc integrity:** Confirmed PRDs (`.docs/prd/`) and finalised Figma designs are the source of truth for _requirements_. `.docs/integration/` docs are guides for _how_ each integration works technically. If a user instruction contradicts either, pause immediately — cite the specific doc, section, and requirement ID — and ask the user whether the doc should be updated or the instruction is a deliberate override. Do not proceed silently either way. The same applies if you spot any improvement or conflict within the docs themselves.

## Living Memory

`.docs/memory/` is the project's persistent memory. Read [.docs/memory/projectState.md](.docs/memory/projectState.md) at the start of every session (or run `/session-start`). For what belongs in each memory file and when to update it, see the [session-start skill](.claude/skills/session-start/SKILL.md).

**Open items that block implementation** are listed under "Unresolved Dependencies" in [.docs/memory/projectState.md](.docs/memory/projectState.md). Ask the user before hard-coding assumptions about any of them.

## 9. Performance Strategy

LCP at p75 mobile is the binding constraint and the de-facto cap on third-party script weight.

| Metric                    | Target |
| ------------------------- | ------ |
| LCP (mobile p75)          | ≤ 2 s  |
| Lighthouse Performance    | ≥ 0.80 |
| Lighthouse Accessibility  | ≥ 0.90 |
| Lighthouse Best Practices | ≥ 0.90 |

### 9.1 Third-party defer rule

Anything loaded via Didomi callback (GTM — which loads Meta, GA4, and other GTM-housed tags via Tell No Lies; Narvar EDD widget; Inside Chat) is deferred, async-loaded, or injected post-hydration so it does not block LCP. **Measmerize** (Find My Size / size guide — PDP only) likewise defers behind LCP — the script injects after the product hero image has loaded. **reCAPTCHA** likewise loads only on register/login form interaction, so it never sits on the critical path of any other page (consent treatment per §11.1). **Exception (AAB-004):** Optimizely Web is a PWA-direct head tag (not a GTM tag) and deliberately loads in the page head **before render** to prevent A/B flicker, scoped to the US storefront where Optimizely runs. **Crazy Egg (AAB-005)** loads async and post-Didomi-consent. Both load strictly post-Didomi-consent; keep both snippets minimal.

### 9.2 Other levers

- **Images:** all storefront imagery — product and editorial — is stored in and served from **Contentful** (`images.ctfassets.net`) via the Contentful Images API; SFCC holds no image assets (DMU-010 migration de-scoped; product images CRM-075; all media via the CMS library HPC-003). The PWA generates `srcset` / `sizes` and sets size, quality, and format per breakpoint on the asset URL — **AVIF primary with WebP / JPEG fallbacks**. Lazy-load all non-LCP images; priority-load the primary hero image (PRD-064). Never render full-resolution images at thumbnail size.
- **Video:** sourced by platform, not self-hosted, so codec / adaptive-streaming selection belongs to the upstream player rather than to this layer:
  - **Product videos → Vimeo**, referenced by embed URL stored in product data or the CMS (PRD-067). Load behind a lightweight facade (poster image + click/scroll-to-load) so the Vimeo player JS never lands on the LCP critical path.
  - **Content-managed page videos → Contentful** by default, served from the Contentful asset CDN and referenced within the CMS content entry alongside the page content. Editorial pages may also embed a Vimeo video by URL where preferred (HPC-004) — the product/editorial split above is the expected pattern, not a hard restriction.
  - Across both: `preload="metadata"` by default; autoplay reserved for muted, short-loop hero clips only.
- Dynamic imports for heavy non-initial components.
- Parallel data fetches; no client-side waterfalls. Fetch only required fields.

### 9.3 Where performance is measured

The CI Lighthouse gate (§14.3) catches regressions but runs against the Dev-tier MRT deployment — slower than production hardware, further from the edge, and not representative of the LCP a real shopper experiences. The signed-off LCP and Lighthouse targets in this section are therefore validated against **Stage**, which mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle size class, same CDN/edge configuration, same SFCC realm tier). Treat CI numbers as regression indicators; treat Stage numbers as the contractual ones.

> **SSR connection pool tuning:** the initial per-pool connection caps defined in §12.1 are derived from expected concurrency, not observed traffic. The first Stage performance run should include per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics (undici emits these as diagnostic channel events). Use those numbers to validate or revise the caps.

---

## 10. Accessibility

**Target:** WCAG 2.2 AA, with WCAG 2.1 AA as the floor that is always met.

**Automated coverage:**

- axe-core via `vitest-axe` at the unit layer and `axe-playwright` at the E2E layer
- Storybook a11y addon at component level during development

## 12. Graceful Degradation

Each external system fails independently — one outage does not break a page.

| System                   | Failure mode                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Contentful               | Render page without editorial content; never block commerce data on CMS                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Global-e                 | Surface explicit error; do not silently fall back to SFCC for international checkout                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Didomi                   | Fail closed — no consent, no third-party scripts                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Omneo (writes) / Emarsys | Queue and retry silently; never block the user flow                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Omneo (reads)            | **Load-bearing for My Account profile pages** — per DMU-004 only email + Omneo ID are migrated; all other customer profile data is sourced live from Omneo at login. Surface an explicit retry/error UI on profile pages if the round-trip fails; do not render stale or partial profile data. |
| Google Maps              | Degrade to manual address entry; never hard-block checkout                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| AP21 (Retail Rewards)    | On AP21 unavailability at the point of Rewards application, inform the customer and allow an alternative payment method                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Narvar (EDD)             | Suppress widget; do not show an error or block checkout                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

### 12.1 Blast-Radius Containment

The failure modes above describe what the PWA does when a single integration is unavailable. This section covers how to limit the _spread_ of an attack or outage — ensuring a degraded integration cannot consume shared resources and take down unrelated features.

#### Edge (outside the PWA — Infrastructure / SI Partner)

- **Web Application Firewalls + rate limiting** is the primary lever for volumetric attacks and credential-stuffing.
- **SFCC Business Manager** provides API-level rate limiting for SFCC endpoints, independent of the storefront edge.

#### SSR layer (inside the PWA)

`overrides/app/ssr.js` makes server-side `fetch` calls directly (token exchange, JWKS, SF Payments metadata). Node's native `fetch` is backed by `undici` internally. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS).

> **Implementation note:** the per-call `dispatcher` option is safer than the `setGlobalDispatcher` in a managed environment (MRT) since it does not touch the global dispatcher that Salesforce internal libraries may rely on. The `commerce-sdk-react` hooks manage their own HTTP client server-side (Commerce SDK) and are not affected in either approach.

The connection pool split is an engineering decision — the right pool boundaries and sizes depend on observed traffic patterns and the integration map in §7. Planned pools (connection caps should be validated later — see §9.3):

| Pool                   | Origin                                                                                                             | Calls                                                                           | Cap | `connectTimeout` | `bodyTimeout` | Reasoning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sfcc-scapi`           | `https://{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com`                                                             | SLAS JWKS (token validation for passwordless login, reset password)             | 5   | 5 s              | 8 s           | `jose` caches the JWK set for its rotation period; actual network calls are rare. Isolated so a JWKS fetch is never starved by higher-volume pools.                                                                                                  |
| `sfcc-payments`        | `config.app.sfPayments.metadataUrl` host (a `*.demandware.net` or SCAPI hostname — waiting confirmation from Mani) | Payment method metadata on every checkout page SSR                              | 10  | 5 s              | 8 s           | Called on every checkout page load; moderate frequency. Separate from `sfcc-scapi` because a checkout traffic spike must not consume SLAS connections.                                                                                               |
| `mulesoft`             | `MULESOFT_BASE_URL`                                                                                                | Order history, order details, boutique / BOPIS stock check, GiveX balance check | 20  | 5 s              | 10 s          | Highest user-facing concurrency (My Account + PDP). GiveX balance calls carry payment credentials in the POST body — a slow MuleSoft response must not hold connections open and starve other pools. Highest cap reflects the broadest call surface. |
| `marketing-cloud-auth` | `https://{subdomain}.auth.marketingcloudapis.com`                                                                  | Marketing Cloud client-credentials token exchange                               | 5   | 5 s              | 15 s          | User-triggered, infrequent; token cached at module scope for 15 min. Isolated so an MC outage cannot consume SFCC or MuleSoft connections.                                                                                                           |
| `marketing-cloud-rest` | `https://{subdomain}.rest.marketingcloudapis.com`                                                                  | Magic-link email send (passwordless login, reset password)                      | 5   | 5 s              | 15 s          | Same trigger as above; higher body timeout because email delivery APIs can respond slowly under load.                                                                                                                                                |
| `google-places`        | `https://places.googleapis.com` (Places API — New)                                                                 | Address autocomplete at checkout (CFD-023, CFD-030, CFD-059)                    | 5   | 3 s              | 5 s           | Non-critical-path; graceful fallback to manual entry. Short timeouts ensure a Places API slowdown releases connections quickly.                                                                                                                      |
| `booxi`                | Booxi base URL (TBD)                                                                                               | Boutique appointment read in My Account (CRM-165–167)                           | 5   | 3 s              | 5 s           | My Account only; non-critical-path within that page.                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Contentful:** The Contentful SDK (`contentful` v11) does not expose a `dispatcher` hook on its internal fetch calls, so connection isolation for Contentful is not achievable through this pattern. Primary mitigation is the graceful degradation rule in §12 (Render page without editorial content).

---

## 13. Testing Strategy

Three layers, no duplicated coverage — the cheapest layer that proves a behaviour wins.

| Layer                 | Tool             | Covers                                               |
| --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Unit                  | Vitest           | Pure logic, data mapping, transforms, isolated hooks |
| Component interaction | Storybook `play` | Single-component user interactions                   |
| E2E                   | Playwright       | Full journeys, multi-region, integration boundaries  |

# Architecture

_Key technical decisions, stack overview, overrides pattern, component organisation, and key paths. Update this file when the stack changes, a new integration is added, or a structural decision is made._

Production storefront for www.zimmermann.com — multi-locale, multi-currency, eight storefronts across six regions (AU, US, UK, EU, HK, ME), with both EU and US each split into two storefronts (domestic + international).

## Pre-Build Decisions

These decisions affect tooling, CI, and code shape that's hard to retrofit later. Status as of 2026-05-29.

| #   | Decision                     | Status                                 |
| --- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| 1   | Browser & device matrix      | ✅ Confirmed (informal)                |
| 2   | Accessibility manual testing | 🟡 Partial — vendor info pending       |
| 3   | Performance budgets          | ✅ Confirmed (informal)                |
| 4   | Client-side error reporting  | ⚪ Accepted risk — no tool             |
| 5   | Feature-flag tool            | ⚪ Accepted risk — Optimizely Web only |
| 6   | Translation fallback chain   | 🟡 Partial — Brand/Legal pending       |

### #1 — Browser & device matrix ✅

**Mobile perf-test floor:** current OS version −2 on iPhone and Android (iOS 17+, Android 14+), verified via BrowserStack Automate. `package.json` browserslist aligned to match.
**Desktop matrix** ([.browserstack.yml](../../.browserstack.yml)): Chrome + Safari (macOS Sonoma), Firefox + Edge (Windows 11) — all latest.

### #2 — Accessibility 🟡

**Target:** WCAG 2.2 AA, at least 2.1 AA. **Automated:** axe-core in Vitest + Playwright; Storybook a11y addon; Lighthouse CI a11y ≥0.90 ([lighthouserc.js](../../lighthouserc.js)). **Manual:** client's existing a11y vendor.
**Pending:** vendor name, screen-reader/browser matrix, audit cadence, remediation owner.

### #3 — Performance budgets ✅

**Client-mandated:** **LCP ≤ 2s** at p75 mobile, plus Lighthouse Performance ≥ 0.80, Accessibility ≥ 0.90, Best Practices ≥ 0.90. These are the only performance numbers in the signed TSD (§9).
**Other CWV (internal working defaults, not client-mandated):** INP ≤ 200ms · CLS ≤ 0.1. Lighthouse mobile defaults at p75.
**CI gate (SIT gate):** Lighthouse CI (`@lhci/cli`) asserts the Lighthouse score floors above, plus a >5pt trend-drop gate (LHCI server required). SEO intentionally not asserted. Runs on every PR to `develop` ([`digital-sit.yml`](../../.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml)), deploys to the **Dev** tier on merge — treat its numbers as a **regression indicator**, not the contractual measurement.
**Contractual measurement:** Client-mandated LCP and Lighthouse numbers are validated on **Stage** — the prod-mimicking tier (same MRT bundle size class, same CDN/edge configuration, same SFCC realm tier as production). The Dev tier is slower and further from the edge, so its absolute numbers will be worse — that is expected and not a sign-off concern. Full environment topology in [tsd-architecture.md §14.1](./temp/tsd-architecture.md).
**Bundle ceilings — internal CI policy, NOT client requirements:** `main.js` 180 kB · `vendor.js` 250 kB · `main.css` 50 kB (`bundlesize` in `package.json`). (These were set as aspirational targets early in the project. As of the last measurement the actual sizes are well above these ceilings (`main.js` ~352 kB, `vendor.js` ~2 MB) before any optimisation pass — the ceilings need to be re-baselined against measured size + a growth-only headroom (e.g. current + 10–15%) once a baseline pass is done.) Their purpose is regression detection, not a client-facing commitment.
**Third-party script weight:** uncapped — tight LCP is the de-facto constraint. See AGENTS.md > Performance for the deferral rule.

### #6 — Translation fallback 🟡

=== 245-290 ===
| **Google Business API**              | Store hours feed (boutique opening hours)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Out-of-band (daily feed into SFCC)                                                                                                                                                            | Consumed by Find in Boutique / store-locator UI — PWA renders, does not call Google directly                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Feedonomics**                      | Product feed for downstream marketing channels (PRD-071)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Out-of-band                                                                                                                                                                                   | No PWA runtime touchpoint; flagged for SEO/marketing dependency awareness only                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Measmerize**                       | Find My Size widget + size guide overlay on PDP (PRD-050–053)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | PWA-direct (script injection on PDP only)                                                                                                                                                     | Browser-direct; no MRT proxy. Script injected once on PDP mount; widget self-determines product availability and signals the PWA via events. Falls back to the Contentful size guide when Measmerize has no data for the product. **Consent approach unconfirmed — open item.**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

## Cross-Storefront Session & Basket Scope

All eight storefronts are path-prefixed on a single first-party domain and share one SFCC realm with shared customer data. The `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie set by the SSR layer is therefore presented on every storefront prefix — no cross-domain SSO bridge is needed. SLAS tokens are channel-scoped, so the SSR layer re-initialises the SLAS context per storefront; a registered shopper is silently re-recognised across a storefront switch (shared customer record), while a guest session is site-scoped and does not carry over. **The basket deliberately does not transfer across storefronts** — baskets are site-scoped and priced in the storefront's own currency/pricebook, so a shopper switching storefront starts a fresh basket. Carrying a basket across a currency boundary would produce incorrect pricing. The Global-e checkout handoff is a separate session boundary (Global-e owns its hosted checkout in full). The exact SLAS re-authorisation mechanism and the stay-signed-in UX are open items with the Salesforce integration team.

## Customer Data Migration (DMU-004, updated 2026-05-29)

Only **email + Omneo customer ID** are migrated into SFCC at go-live. All other customer profile data — name, phone, addresses, communication preferences — is sourced **live from Omneo at login** via MuleSoft. Implication: My Account profile pages cannot rely on SFCC for the full customer record; an Omneo round-trip is required post-authentication. Graceful degradation for Omneo outages becomes load-bearing on account screens. Asset/CDN migration (DMU-010) is **de-scoped** — images stay in Contentful, no asset 301s.

## Blast-Radius Mitigation

Multiple upstream integrations (SFCC, MuleSoft/Omneo, Global-e, Narvar, Contentful, Didomi, Inside Chat) mean a failure or attack targeting one service must not cascade. A PWA-relevant mitigation can be done in the SSR layer.

The SSR layer in `overrides/app/ssr.js` uses **Node's native `fetch`**, which is backed by `undici`. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS).

```ts
import { Pool } from 'undici';

// 1. Create isolated pools for specific origins
const checkoutPool = new Pool('https://api.checkout-service.com', {
  connections: 10, // Hard limit of 10 concurrent connections to this origin
  timeout: 8000,
});

// 2. Use them explicitly in your fetch calls inside ssr.js
async function getCheckoutMetadata() {
  return await fetch('https://api.checkout-service.com/v1/metadata', {
    dispatcher: checkoutPool, // Safely isolated!
  });
}
```

The connection pool split is an engineering decision — the right pool boundaries and sizes depend on observed traffic patterns and the integration map in §7. Planned pools (connection caps should be validated later — see §9.3):

| Pool                   | Origin                                                                                                            | Calls                                                                           | Cap | `connectTimeout` | `bodyTimeout` | Reasoning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sfcc-scapi`           | `https://{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com`                                                            | SLAS JWKS (token validation for passwordless login, reset password)             | 5   | 5 s              | 8 s           | `jose` caches the JWK set for its rotation period; actual network calls are rare. Isolated so a JWKS fetch is never starved by higher-volume pools.                                                                                                  |
| `sfcc-payments`        | `config.app.sfPayments.metadataUrl` host (a `*.demandware.net` or SCAPI hostname — confirm with Integration team) | Payment method metadata on every checkout page SSR                              | 10  | 5 s              | 8 s           | Called on every checkout page load; moderate frequency. Separate from `sfcc-scapi` because a checkout traffic spike must not consume SLAS connections.                                                                                               |
| `mulesoft`             | `MULESOFT_BASE_URL`                                                                                               | Order history, order details, boutique / BOPIS stock check, GiveX balance check | 20  | 5 s              | 10 s          | Highest user-facing concurrency (My Account + PDP). GiveX balance calls carry payment credentials in the POST body — a slow MuleSoft response must not hold connections open and starve other pools. Highest cap reflects the broadest call surface. |
| `marketing-cloud-auth` | `https://{subdomain}.auth.marketingcloudapis.com`                                                                 | Marketing Cloud client-credentials token exchange                               | 5   | 5 s              | 15 s          | User-triggered, infrequent; token cached at module scope for 15 min. Isolated so an MC outage cannot consume SFCC or MuleSoft connections.                                                                                                           |
| `marketing-cloud-rest` | `https://{subdomain}.rest.marketingcloudapis.com`                                                                 | Magic-link email send (passwordless login, reset password)                      | 5   | 5 s              | 15 s          | Same trigger as above; higher body timeout because email delivery APIs can respond slowly under load.                                                                                                                                                |
| `google-places`        | `https://places.googleapis.com` (Places API — New)                                                                | Address autocomplete at checkout (CFD-023, CFD-030, CFD-059)                    | 5   | 3 s              | 5 s           | Non-critical-path; graceful fallback to manual entry. Short timeouts ensure a Places API slowdown releases connections quickly.                                                                                                                      |
| `booxi`                | Booxi base URL (TBD — confirm with Integration team)                                                              | Boutique appointment read in My Account (CRM-165–167)                           | 5   | 3 s              | 5 s           | My Account only; non-critical-path within that page.                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

## 5. Multi-Site, Multi-Locale Architecture

### 5.1 Storefronts

**8 independent SFCC sites across 6 regions**, each with its own currency, tax model, locale set, delivery options, and payment methods. 11 active locales total. US/EU domestic and international are configured as separate SFCC sites (REG-006).

| Locale                          | URL prefix                                 | Currency               | Checkout owner          |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- | ----------------------- |
| AU + Oceania                    | `/` (x-default hreflang)                   | AUD                    | SFCC (REG-003)          |
| UK                              | `/uk/`                                     | GBP                    | SFCC (REG-004)          |
| US domestic                     | `/us/`                                     | USD                    | SFCC (REG-005)          |
| US international                | `/en-ca/`                                  | USD                    | Global-e (REG-005)      |
| EU domestic — EN / FR / IT / ES | `/en-eu/`, `/fr-eu/`, `/it-eu/`, `/es-eu/` | EUR                    | SFCC (REG-006 dom)      |
| EU international                | `/en-ch/`                                  | EUR                    | Global-e (REG-006 intl) |
| HK                              | `/hk/`                                     | HKD (Global-e display) | Global-e (REG-007)      |
| ME                              | `/en-ae/`                                  | AED (Global-e display) | Global-e (REG-008)      |

Rest-of-world traffic routes via `/en-ch/` and `/en-ca/` (DMU-013). AU is configured at the root with no locale prefix and serves as the x-default hreflang target (DMU-016).

### 5.2 Entry routing

- **IP geolocation** selects the site on first visit (REG-013).
- **AU is gated** to Oceania IPs only (REG-009) but remains the x-default hreflang target, so gating runs in the application layer rather than at the network. Non-Oceania human visitors are redirected server-side to their matched storefront before AUD pricing renders; verified search-engine and social-unfurler bots are exempt; UA ambiguity fails open (false positives have no SEO cost; missing a real crawler does).
- **Cross-region entry handling for all other storefronts** — first-visit mismatch-detection slide-out, the country/language selector, and the EU language-mismatch modal — is functional design (REG-014–035), out of scope for this TSD.

### 5.3 Single source of truth for country / locale

Country, locale, currency, shipping country, Global-e flag, and boutique-region data live in a single front-end configuration module. When a market is added, that module and the SFCC site configuration are updated together.

### 5.4 Per-storefront concerns that must not bleed

- **Consent defaults (REG-054):** per-storefront Didomi defaults are site-scoped config that must not bleed across storefronts; the values themselves are specified under REG-054.
- **Tax model:** SFCC native tax tables (AU GST, UK VAT); Avalara for US domestic, NZ, New Caledonia, and EU domestic (EU domestic added 2026-06-19); Global-e handles tax for international checkout paths.
- **Marketing opt-in default (REG-057):** site-scoped per storefront; must not bleed — value specified under REG-057.
- **Payment methods:** per-storefront Adyen configuration. Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Klarna are post-launch.

### 5.5 Session and basket scope across storefronts

All eight storefronts are path-prefixed on a single first-party domain and run on a single SFCC realm with shared customer data. This determines how a shopper's session behaves when they cross storefronts (via the country / language selector or the mismatch slide-out):

- **Session cookie is shared.** The `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie set by the SSR layer is first-party to the one domain, so it is presented on requests to any storefront prefix — no cross-domain SSO bridge is needed.
- **Tokens are channel-scoped.** A SLAS token carries the site it was issued for, so the SSR layer re-initialises the SLAS context for the destination storefront. Because the customer record is shared across the realm, a registered shopper is silently re-recognised without re-entering credentials; a guest session is site-scoped and does not carry over.
- **Basket does not transfer — by design.** Baskets are site-scoped and priced in the storefront's own currency against its own pricebook, so a shopper switching storefront starts a fresh basket. Carrying a basket across a currency / pricebook boundary would produce incorrect pricing.
- **Checkout handoff is separate.** When an international storefront hands off to Global-e, the SLAS session does not extend into the Global-e hosted checkout — Global-e owns that session in full.

---

## 6. Checkout Ownership Branching

Checkout owner is determined at PDP / cart, not only at the checkout page — so price, shipping, duty, and tax presentation are correct before the customer commits.

- **SFCC owns:** AU domestic (including Oceania — Avalara for NZ + New Caledonia), UK, US (when shipping to US), EU domestic.
- **Global-e owns:** HK, ME, EU international, the US site when shipping outside the US, and any domestic storefront when the selected shipping destination is outside that storefront's market.

## 14. CI/CD & Environments

This section probably belong to a DevOps TSD, but will put here temporarily until we have one.

### 14.1 Topology

A six-tier environment topology spans **Local → Dev → SIT → UAT → Stage → Prod**. Each tier (other than Local) has its own SFCC realm, Contentful environment, and MuleSoft connections. Ownership splits across three zones — Digital, IT/NewStore, and Shared (Digital + Business).

| #   | Tier            | Owner         | Purpose                                                                      | Third-party availability                                              | Deploy trigger                                                              |
| --- | --------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **Local**       | Digital       | Feature build on developer machines                                          | All services mocked (MSW stubs)                                       | `npm start`                                                                 |
| 2   | **Dev**         | Digital       | Integrated digital testing across all 6 storefronts, independent of NewStore | MuleSoft STG · NewStore Dev · Omneo STG · Narvar stub · Adyen sandbox | Merge to `develop`                                                          |
| 3   | **SIT**         | IT / NewStore | NewStore SIT and regression on its own cadence                               | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Narvar STG · AP21 test                  | NewStore release cadence (parallel lane, non-blocking for Digital releases) |
| 4   | **UAT**         | Shared        | Business acceptance across all 6 regions                                     | NewStore STG · Narvar STG · Omneo STG · Adyen sandbox                 | Business approval gate                                                      |
| 5   | **Stage** (E2E) | Shared        | End-to-end testing with all third parties live; time-boxed booked windows    | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Omneo STG · Narvar STG · Adyen sandbox  | Booked 2-week window                                                        |
| 6   | **Prod**        | Live          | Production; AU canary then flag-flip to remaining regions                    | NewStore PROD · MuleSoft PROD · Omneo PROD · Narvar PROD · Adyen PROD | Release manager + canary gate                                               |

Stage is the **contractual performance-test environment** referenced in §9.3 — it mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle class, CDN/edge configuration, SFCC realm tier).

### 14.2 Branch model

GitFlow with explicit back-merges to keep `develop` aligned with production.

| Branch                    | Branched from          | Merges to                                                                       |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `feature/*`               | `develop`              | `develop`                                                                       |
| `fix/*`                   | `develop`              | `develop`                                                                       |
| `release/*`               | `develop`              | `main` **and** `develop`                                                        |
| `fix/release-{version}-*` | the `release/*` branch | the `release/*` branch (forward-merged to `develop` via the release back-merge) |
| `hotfix/*`                | `main`                 | `main` **and** `develop`                                                        |
| `develop`, `main`         | —                      | protected; PR-only                                                              |

Release branches are supervised — code logic fixes go on a `fix/release-{version}-*` sub-branch rather than directly on the release branch. Releases and hotfixes always back-merge to `develop` so production fixes flow forward automatically.

### 14.3 CI workflows

**QA workflow (`qa.yml`)** — runs on every PR to `develop` and `release/**`. Code-correctness checks with no environment dependency:

- Unit tests (Vitest)
- Storybook interaction tests (`play` functions) and component-level accessibility checks via `@storybook/addon-a11y` (`storybook test --ci`)

**SIT gate (`digital-sit.yml`)** — runs on push/PR to `release/**`; on merge to `develop` it also deploys to the **Dev** environment (tier 2 in §14.1). Environment-dependent checks:

- Playwright `p0` priority specs
- Bundle-size check against the ceilings in §9
- Contract tests against the MuleSoft OpenAPI specification
- Lighthouse CI thresholds (Performance ≥ 0.80, Accessibility ≥ 0.90, Best Practices ≥ 0.90)
- Trend gate against the LHCI history server

### 14.4 Deployment

Deployment is via Salesforce Managed Runtime. Each tier maps to its own MRT target:

- **Dev** — deployed on merge to `develop`, gated on a clean SIT gate (§14.3)
- **SIT** — deployed on the NewStore release cadence, isolated from the Digital release path (failures do not block `release/**`)
- **UAT** — deployed for business acceptance; promotion requires Business sign-off
- **Stage** — deployed on a booked 2-week window for full end-to-end testing with live third parties
- **Prod** — release-manager-gated; AU canary first, then flag-flip to remaining regions

Production deploys are gated on a clean SIT gate run plus stakeholder approval through UAT and Stage.

MRT deployment targets map one-to-one to the topology: `dev | sit | uat | stage | production`.

38:## Bundles
40:The storefront code that runs on an environment is called a **bundle**. Use the developer tools included in PWA Kit to generate a bundle and push it to Managed Runtime.
43:A bundle is a snapshot of your code at a specific point in time. It’s *immutable*: After a bundle has been created, it can’t be changed. Having this complete and accurate history of bundles makes troubleshooting deployments easier.
46:After pushing the bundle, you can use the Runtime Admin or Managed Runtime API to designate that bundle as “deployed.” Each project can have multiple bundles, but each environment can have only one bundle that's designated as deployed.
